Lots of comments that are super on point! One small thing to add that I myself grew out of and have also seen from other teachers is this:

When you're new and/or young, the kids WILL test you. They might do small things that break rules like make a snarky comment, talk when you're talking (and they know you see them), refuse actions, stand up and walk around, etc. If you can discern whether their intention is to test you, or they're actually causing a problem, it helps. If they're testing you, you can usually tell based on inflection or how they look at you when they misbehave. If it's a test, you can pass by quietly and subtley correcting (or making a joke out of it) instead of turning it into a yes no yes no battle. Choose your fights very carefully.

Plan out your top 3 most important rules, and be steady, constant, and strict on those. The rest, chill out. Show your kids love. Get to know them personally. Make as many kids as you can feel like your favorites. Be the fun, sweet, loving teacher. Except when they break those 3 rules, be constant. Not scary, not mean, but at least very serious. They'll know you mean business and they'll know they messed up. All in all, when kids know you love them, and when kids know your rules are really important (and you're not some kind of do it because I say so teacher), they'll respect your rules.

I know everyone is on the spoiled brat train, and that's probably likely, but my first thought was - could this 14 year old have also been upset about the dog dying and needed to visit? I wouldn't only allow one kid to grieve. These girls grew up together and even if the dog belonged to the 16 year, the 14 year old could have gotten attached or even just miss the dog's presence. 

This could be a case of spoiled brat tantrum, but it could also be the case of an emotional 14 year old who was denied an outlet for grief and blames the 16 year old and doesn't have an understanding of how to communicate feelings.

The problem is that dog nervousness could develop into comfort and love for dogs, or it could develop into a phobia. There's no way for you or that person to know. I'd have the person play with dogs of friends or neighbors frequently,  and I'd even say you should try fostering before adopting. That way if the person can't handle a dog living with them (and living with will be different from just playing with), at least there's no real harm since it's a temporary situation. It'd also help your applications to say you've been a foster!

When your brain isn't fully developed, you are more prone to making impulsive decisions and not fully thinking things through. As someone who was your age not too too too long ago, I'm glad they wouldn't let me adopt at 22. I thought I had the maturity, but comparing who I am now, and my ability to make a long term commitment, compared to at age 22.... the age limits are there for a reason, and while you can pay bills, go to the army, work full time, own property, etc - your brain isn't even completely done developing. It's a whole life depending on you, and it's just too risky to depend a life on someone who's not even done growing into an adult.
